nodes.description: An age-dependent susceptibility to occipital epileptic activity is inferred from visual seizure semiology, occipital EEG abnormalities, absence of a causal MRI lesion and frequent remission during maturation. The responsible molecular and cellular changes are unresolved. Nonoccipital EEG abnormalities can coexist, so the susceptibility is not necessarily confined to the occipital lobe.

nodes.description: Antiseizure medication is commonly used during the active phase because untreated seizures can be frequent. Many patients respond to monotherapy. Historical cohort response differs between isolated COVE and COVE associated with other epilepsy syndromes, but the available abstract does not provide denominators for comparing response percentages. These sources do not establish one drug as superior for COVE.

nodes.description: In patients with fixation-off sensitivity, removing central vision facilitates epileptiform discharges and restoring fixation suppresses them. This is principally a reflex EEG phenomenon. Its expression varies across patients and it occurs in other epilepsies; it is not established as the trigger of habitual COVE seizures. Proposed links to alpha-rhythm circuitry are physiological interpretations rather than a demonstrated COVE-specific cellular pathway.

nodes.description: A prospective open-label pilot enrolled 12 children and adolescents with Gastaut-type childhood occipital epilepsy. Eleven were seizure-free at six months, and all were seizure-free at 12 and 18 months. This small uncontrolled study supports possible effectiveness and tolerability, but does not establish superiority, a universal response rate or disease modification.

nodes.description: At seizure onset, the usual interictal occipital spikes may diminish as unilateral occipital fast rhythms with low-amplitude spikes emerge. Slower ictal spike-and-wave activity can accompany blindness or oculoclonic seizures. This evolving ictal pattern is distinct from interictal FOS-related paroxysms.

nodes.description: Occipital sharp waves or spike-and-wave complexes occur between seizures, sometimes only in sleep. Sleep and sleep deprivation enhance their detection; FOS can also facilitate them. These interictal abnormalities are distinguished from the evolving ictal rhythm and do not by themselves establish that a clinical seizure is occurring.

nodes.description: Occipital seizure activity disrupts visual processing, producing positive visual phenomena or transient visual loss. Elementary colored circles are typical, but complex hallucinations and illusions can occur. Semiology supports involvement of visual networks without proving exclusive recruitment of striate cortex or a specific cellular activation-versus-suppression mechanism.
